extracted.intended_audience: media/journalism researchers, journalism students, and news professionals interested in news selection and news values
extracted.subtask_description: A taxonomy of news values used to evaluate/select events for news coverage, listing and defining the many criteria (e.g., size, negativity, prominence, novelty, proximity, timeliness, human interest, etc.) that influence newsworthiness. Intended as an academic reference and practical guide to how events are judged newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size / Scale / Threshold (superlativeness; magnitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events measured by the level of size, scale or scope: 'the bigger... more violent [the event is] the bigger the headlines it will make' and 'there is a threshold the event will have to pass before it will be recorded at all.' Size covers quantification/estimation of number of people/places/things affected and that events must be of a scale large enough to warrant attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the biggest building, the most violent crime, the most destructive fire gets covered' (Galtung & Ruge's THRESHOLD). 'Stories that are perceived as sufficiently significant either in the numbers of people involved or in potential impact.' Notes that slow processes (e.g., climate change) become newsworthy only when they 'go critical' and condense to a bounded event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity / Discontinuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are temporally sharp or show a sudden deviation from the norm are easier to integrate into the news cycle ('The sharper and more temporally bounded the event the easier it is to integrate it into the temporal rhythms of news').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to distinguish slow, steady phenomena from newsworthy, bounded events (e.g., coastal erosion vs. an acute flood). Relates to news cycle and novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity / Conflict / Deviance / Drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative news is preferred to positive news because it often satisfies selection criteria better, is more consensual and unambiguous, and is more unexpected. Negativity includes violence, crime, conflict, disaster, scandal, and deviance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes and examples: 'Bad news is good news... News is about disruptions' ; examples include 'act of violence, hostages, warlike incident, murder', 'protest, demonstration, strike', 'stories about violent crimes, murder, battles and wars'. Conflict dramatizes stories by matching opposed viewpoints. 'If it bleeds it leads.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Valence: Success / Positivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive change, satisfactory completion, restoration or success can itself be a news value: 'stories with particularly positive overtones such as rescues and cures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers 'good news' items that demonstrate successful outcomes or positive developments and may be used especially to balance bulletins or as human-interest pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance / Impact / Relevance / Consequence (social significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events are newsworthy if they have considerable significance for large numbers of people — if they affect lives, living conditions, finances, education, future, etc. ('Usually taken to mean that the reported event has considerable significance for large numbers of people in the audience').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called social impact, importance, consequence or significance. Journalists often equate impact with newsworthiness: 'the bigger the impact, the bigger the story.' Personalization of impact is a common presentation technique to show relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recency / Timeliness / Currency / Topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement that news be up to date and refer to events as close to transmission/publication time as possible: 'the best news is something which has only just happened.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drivers: competitive pressure to be first (the 'scoop') and the periodicity of news production. Timeliness can also include anniversaries, seasonal stories, or whether a new comment adds to an ongoing debate ('Is it new, current, immediately relevant?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity / Identification / Cultural closeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical, cultural or psychological nearness of an event to the audience: 'local and ideological proximity of news events' and 'interpretable within the cultural framework of the listener or reader.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proximity includes geographic closeness, cultural familiarity/ethnocentrism and other ties (historical, social, financial). 'Nearby events take precedence over similar events at a distance.' Distant events may be made relevant through local angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance / Expectation / Predictability / Stereotype
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that correspond to what audiences and journalists expect or what fits shared norms and scripts are more likely to be selected: 'News should be consonant with socially-shared norms, values, and attitudes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes expected event types (press conference, state visit) and compatibility with preconceptions about actors or nations. Even unexpected events can assume 'familiar contours' in coverage through established scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / Unexpectedness / Surprise / Deviance
rubrics_metrics.description: The unexpected, rare, or unusual is more newsworthy than the routine. Novelty can be statistical deviance (rarity), normative deviance (violating norms), or 'pathological deviance' (threatening the status quo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the old man-bites-dog syndrome.' Novelty may conflict with prevailing wisdom or 'stretch credulity.' It can relate to incidents, viewpoints, lifestyles or conditions; routine events are less likely to be reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence / Eliteness / Celebrity / Status
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning elite people, powerful organizations, or high-status nations receive greater notice: 'the actions of the elite are... more consequential' and 'big names are better news than nobodies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes heads of state, major institutions, celebrities and acknowledged experts. Prominence can also derive from recognisability at local to international levels and the public interest in private lives of public figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization / Personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Making stories about people (individuals) increases newsworthiness by providing identification and comprehension: 'News is about people, and mostly about individuals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personification helps dramatize and concretize processes or institutions by reducing them to individual actions or experiences. Factors reinforcing personification include photographability and fit with news frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human interest / Entertainment / Emotional appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with emotional, touching, amusing or entertaining components attract audiences ('An event with emotional, touching aspects...'). Often associated with feature/soft stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes stories about sex, showbusiness, animals, heroes, rescues, and items that 'tug at the heartstrings.' Linked to novelty and personalization; can span humorous to tragic incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that arouses strong emotion or is dramatized for effect: 'short, dramatic occurrences which can be sensationalized' and definitions that emphasize 'emotion arousing' aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensationalist packaging may amplify drama and audience reaction; considered a distinct decision factor though ethically fraught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity / Clarity / Simplification / Brevity (news-writing objectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: News favours items that are clear, unambiguous, and simple to present; stories should be tightly packed with facts and easily understood within the news format ('the less ambiguity the more the event will be noticed').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines include providing necessary background/presupposed information, presenting facts clearly and concisely (brevity is vital for broadcast and print space constraints), and ensuring the story 'contains enough background and explicit reference to be understood on its own.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition / Balance / Story mix
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors seek a balanced mix of stories across types, geographies and subjects and consider how an item fits with surrounding items ('the desire to present a ‘balanced’ whole').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider story mixture by subject, geography, demography and internal 'fit' (e.g., packaging a local angle on a national story). Bulletins may be ordered to manage tone (ending with upbeat human-interest items) and to avoid duplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: News agenda / News cycle dynamics (frequency, continuity, follow-up; the news barrier)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the timing, frequency and presence of items in the ongoing news agenda affect selection: events whose frequency matches the medium are more likely to be recorded; once in the news, issues tend to stay ('once something has hit the headlines... it will continue to be defined as news').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes the 'news barrier' idea: simplicity, personalization and excitement help an item pass into ongoing coverage. Follow-ups, thematic continuity and availability of 'ready-made text' also increase likelihood of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: External / Organisational factors: Competition, commercial pressures, organisational requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Market and organisational conditions shape coverage choices: outlets compete for exclusives; commercial pressures (circulation/readership) and structural effects influence story selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: every outlet wants an exclusive; stories compete for limited space/time. Organisational needs (format, budget, staffing) and advertiser/owner pressures can distort selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other factors: Uncertainty, Facticity, Secrecy, Suspense, Episodicity and format constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Various additional factors influence newsworthiness: uncertainty about future consequences, degree of factual detail (names, sums, locations), secrecy (leaks), suspense (what will happen next), episodic character (beginning and end within a day) and medium/format constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Event with reference to the future of which consequences are unclear' makes news; 'degree to which a story contains the kinds of facts and figures on which hard news thrives' (facticity); secrecy/leaks are newsworthy. These often interact with temporal and novelty factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual attractiveness / Picture opportunity (visual news values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual qualities of an event or available footage/photography increase newsworthiness: 'A story may be included simply because film is available or because of the dramatic qualities of the film.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms: visual attractiveness, picture opportunity. Visuals can drive inclusion even if other values are weaker; photographic drama, availability of film, or striking images enhance selection.
